item.title: Teucris
item.description: Accept, but do not condone, the dying of the light
item.dc:creator: Andy Tang
item.content:encoded:
O fortes peioraque passi mecum saepe viri,
nunc vino pellite curas;
cras ingens iterabimus aequor

O brave men, who have often borne with me great sorrow,
now drive away your cares with wine;
Tomorrow, we shall set out again upon the vast ocean.

— Teucer, in Horace, Odes 1.7.29-31

In Greek literature and mythology, there’s a pretty well-known term of hubris, describing a transgression and the consequences that follow. The Erinyes pursue those who swear a false oath. Figures like Ajax the Lesser or Arachne dared to challenge the gods and hence were slain for it. Oedipus seeks to avoid his own fate, only to walk into it. No one is too clever to avoid the fruits of hubris.

Certainly, such a perspective would be advantageous in antiquity. An ancient farmer would gain nothing from challenging Fate over the destruction of a harvest or a sudden plague. But in this era of science, we have conquered plagues and delivered billions from famine. “To Mars we’ll go,” exclaims the industrialist as our species tests the limits of the planet that bore us. Chemists and physicists labor to understand so that engineers may innovate new weapons that let us conquer space, time, death itself.

Is hubris now vestigial, a concept which has outlived its usefulness? Not so. For our capability for destruction has advanced apace with our innovations. We live in a world without smallpox, yet nuclear annihilation hangs over our heads like the double-edged Sword of Damocles. We have created man-made horrors beyond the comprehension of any ancient hero.

But there are more flavors now to what hubris once was, not all negative. How might we distinguish the dikes of Yu the Great from tilting at windmills? I think the former bears with it some intrinsic recognition of reality both present and future. We build dams or engineer our crops because it’s a plausible means of making the world more just, more verdant, than the way things were. I am reminded of this rallying blog post: “The world is awful. The world is much better. The world could be much better.”

And indeed—between the waves of hubris in the Iliad, there is a hero in whom this hope survived, without the divine favor of Odysseus or Diomedes. After Troy fell, the archer Teucris refused to depart before his brother Ajax was buried, despite his shameful suicide. After arriving home, he was banished for this same reason, for his father held the proper action would have been to return Ajax home. Horace wrote that he acknowledged his fate, beseeching his companions to “drown their sorrows in wine,” and yet even in his darkest hour he looked to a dawn more welcoming.

May there be Teucris in our futures then: we have so often borne great sorrow, but behold! Tomorrow we shall set sail across the vast ocean.

item.title: In the Cold and the Dark
item.description: To those I have lost, am losing, and am yet to lose
item.dc:creator: Andy Tang
item.content:encoded:
Man cannot live without a permanent trust in something indestructible in himself, and at the same time that indestructible something as well as his trust in it may remain permanently concealed from him.

— Franz Kafka

There is something terrible about the silence of a winter forest. Imagine: before agriculture, before any tools much more sophisticated than a stone flake axe, one of your ancestors’ cousins must have gotten lost in a place just like this. They have given up retracing their steps in circles. They have given up calling for their tribe.

Linguists have no records from the Mesolithic, but certainly they would have had a name: call him Sethur. For days Sethur has been hiking. He has no warmth save the fire he lights each night and no water save for the snow he melts. Far in the distance the wolves howl, but when the sleek predators come they are silent. He has already been attacked twice, bitten once—he is tired.

As the shadows lengthen again every dark place seems to hide danger. But Sethur is a man of the hunt: it will take more than hunger or exposure or gangrene to lay him low. What happens over the next week is a far more internal struggle. There is nothing to tell him how far he has journeyed, no mirror in which to see his face. He hikes and fights on. When he reaches the next village, will he still be proud Sethur, killer of a dozen wild boars? And should he perish: would his willpower die before his body did?

Winter is a time of change: all living things adapt to its harshness. The mighty oak sheds its leaves. Bears slumber for months. Butterflies and birds alike fly thousands of miles to evade the cold. You and I change too—but maybe it happens too gradually for us to notice.

Winter is a time of meditation. It awakens me from the nonstop rush of my studies to imagine stories of wolves and ancestors, to touch upon what anchors me to this world. I am sure every living thing is born with or makes themselves this will to endure: I am sure you have or had it too. I wish I could tell you that your fire within, much more than cold laurels and medals, will bring you through your winter. That the simple act of fighting to endure makes you “worthy” more than whatever definition you made up.

Winter tests you. The way will be long. It is unknown, maybe unknowable, where the next village is. You will fall short, you will attempt impossibilities: there is no shame in any of this. Just know that the act of trying will save you. Step by step, you will walk into a spring that you had all but forgotten.

My friend: the world has failed you in many ways it has not failed me. Maybe I have failed you, or am failing you, or will fail you. Maybe it’s been one month or five years. Maybe I’d know the exact address to send this letter, or maybe it will rest with flowers at your grave. But know that there is unbreakable salvation within you.

Know that you are the master of your own fate.

Know that I remember who you were, or will remember who you are.

Know that you were or are more important than you’ll ever know.

Know that people miss you, or will miss you.

Know that you are loved.

AYT

item.title: A Web of 68,396 NeurIPS Citations
item.description: Recovering topic-level structure from graph clusters
item.dc:creator: Andy Tang
item.content:encoded:
Before I flew back to the Midwest for winter break, I met up with a friend of mine who’d been gone most of finals week for NeurIPS ‘23. For those not in the machine learning field, NeurIPS is one of the most prestigious conferences in the field, and the one takeaway I had from that conference was that it had become colossal. How massive? Given my sudden windfall of free time, I decided to map it out.

Aggregate Statistics

I first catalogued all NeurIPS papers indexed in Semantic Scholar, allowing me to chart out how many papers were published per year.

I then spent two nights hammering the Semantic Scholar citations API, allowing me to retrieve a mostly accurate* picture of each paper’s references. I turned these references into a huge edge list (published here, see note on inaccuracies below) and ran Gephi’s graph edge visualizer to produce the beautiful image above. Immediately I was struck by the substructure apparent in the ForceAtlas layout of the graph and went to investigate further—this is going to be a picture-heavy post.

For a brief sanity check I showed the distribution of the number of NeurIPS papers cited by each NeurIPS paper. These skew on the lower end, with about half the papers citing less than four other papers from previous conference proceedings.

*Notably I figured out that in fact some NeurIPS papers did cite more than 100 sources, meaning I need to re-aggregate data to take that factor into account. Will update this post when that’s complete!

Most NeurIPS papers are also not cited by many other NeurIPS papers. We see many papers with zero NeurIPS citations: one could expect this to contain all 2,834 papers from 2022, which accounts for nearly half that number. A few papers are cited by an exceptional number of other submissions: let’s find out which ones!

Top and Recent Papers

The #1 paper is, understandably, Attention Is All You Need (2017) with 1014 citations, followed by the PyTorch paper (2019) with 720 citations. Citations drop by a factor of two for third place, Language Models are Few-Shot Learners (2020), with 353. Notably, these papers all are in the same dense neighborhood, raising the question as to what defines these neighborhoods in the first place. Two hypotheses come to mind:

  1. Neighborhoods are defined by the age of the work: works which are hyper-cited tend to draw works that post-date them into their neighborhood.

  2. Neighborhoods are defined by the subfield of work that’s being done, with works in the same subfield more likely to cite each other.

These are testable hypotheses! I wrote a script to label all points by year of publication and colored all data points after 2017 (publication of “Attention Is All You Need”) in cyan. The result is shown below:

We see a wide distribution of cyan on our image, showing that our hypothesis is at least not totally correct. There is a conspicuous lack of cyan in specific outlying parts of the graph, though—more on that later. The logical next step is to analyze the properties of works neighboring each other. From now on, the attention and PyTorch papers will be highlighted as references so you know what part of the graph you’re looking at. All analysis will also be done from the non-rotated graph.

Subscribe now

Neighborhood Analyses

Out of curiosity, I choose Diffusion Improves Graph Learning as my reference paper, which has only been cited by 23 other NeurIPS papers. Since this focuses on graph neural nets and diffusion, I expect it to be somewhat far from the attention paper. Nevertheless, upon analysis it falls within the same large area. After a query, I find the large dot next to it (also highlighed in cyan) is Inductive Representation Learning on Large Graphs, suggesting that that neighborhood represents work in GNNs. What about clusters apart from the main cluster?

The paper highlighted at far right is Random Features for Large-Scale Kernel Machines (2007). The cluster around it has few recent papers, as shown in the cyan visualization, which makes sense since deep learning has mostly displaced kernel methods in current work. The one below, more embedded in recent papers, is Neural Tangent Kernel: Convergence and Generalization in Neural Networks (2018), which links kernel methods with neural networks. Since this work focuses both on deep learning and kernel methods, it makes sense that it’s surrounded by newer papers and about equidistant between the large deep learning cluster and the kernel cluster. What about outlying papers at the top of the map?

In brown I highlight the classic Sutton paper: Policy Gradient Methods for Reinforcement Learning with Function Approximation (1999). Even further out, and cited 161 times, is Improved Algorithms for Linear Stochastic Bandits (2011). This seems to suggest that the northern arm on this map is a cluster of reinforcement learning papers, especially classic RL results not paired with deep learning.

Recap

Here’s what we’ve found so far:

  • NeurIPS papers are densely connected by co-citations (98% are in the largest connected component, and network diameter is 18).

  • While most papers only cite or are cited by few NeurIPS papers, a few heavy-hitters have hundreds or thousands of citations at the conference.

  • A ForceAtlas 2 layout of the graph exposes clusters which, upon inspection, correlate closely with specific areas of study. These clusters tend not to correlate with publication year.

To my knowledge, this is the first exploration of the citation graph structure of an academic conference. I wonder if the underlying structure could be used to better explore existing literature: arXiv is notoriously colossal, and I don’t know anyone who actively uses Connected Papers. I hope this data, in the hands of the right person, will improve the discoverability of vast amounts of scientific insight.

item.title: Finding Parts is the Hardest Part
item.description: Reflections on what robotics can teach us
item.dc:creator: Andy Tang
item.content:encoded:
The beginning is perhaps more difficult than anything else, but keep heart, it will turn out all right.

― Vincent van Gogh (source)

What does it take for a robot to play badminton? This year, I spent my Thanksgiving afternoons finding out. Before break, I made a list of things that had to be done:

  • Chassis construction, a problem best solved with existing mecanum chassis

  • Arm design, requiring rapid prototyping via laser-cutter and 3D printing

  • Electronic control, which could be done via remote control

  • Autonomous control, requiring computer vision and Arduino programming

The project seemed simple enough, and it wasn’t even particularly novel: students in Vietnam, where the game is more culturally mainstream, had built such a bot a few years ago. Nevertheless, I felt mired in creative quicksand, agonizing over miniscule decisions. I got out of my slump in the usual way: with a credit card.

With the gracious support of Stanford Student Robotics, I went on a shopping spree, purchasing around $1200 of basic materials and a week’s worth of snacks. From there it was smooth sailing. I announced our goal, trained seven or eight people on mechanical techniques, and finished the robot (minus computer vision) in five days.

This experience is surprisingly common in robotics: an alum once told me that “80% of robotics is online shopping.” So what makes finding parts so hard?

The difficulty in buying parts, especially for the uninitiated, is the paradox of choice. Once you open Amazon, or even McMaster-Carr, you’re presented with a paralyzing infinity of choices. You spend so long agonizing over whether to buy M3 or M4 screws that you forget you don’t need perfect, just good enough. And “good enough” can be quite hacky—for all my horror about my lab drilling M3 wood screws into the M2 holes of our $3,000 Go1 robot dog, it got the job done.

I think another part of this problem is that parts give your project an air of finality. You feel like you’re constraining yourself to one specific vision of the solution—and indeed, the types of parts you can 3D-print or laser cut are limited. The mistake is thinking that oversights are fatal: they aren’t, and all you have to do to get over them is to order more parts.

If we broaden our definition of “parts,” I think we can extend our analysis of project difficulty beyond robotics (where others may not be so lucky to have an infinite piggy-bank of parts). Briefly, I categorize all projects into three categories:

  1. Theoretical: such as mathematical research, initial synthesis of chemical compounds, or machine learning methods/architecture (such as LLMs, diffusion models, and reinforcement learning). These are characterized by new ways of thinking designed to solve novel problems.

  2. Applied: such as quantum computing, manufacture of chemicals at scale, or machine learning augmentations (e.g. chain-of-thought, fine-tuning, RAGs). These implement theory to create new capabilities in existing tools.

  3. Commercial/Industrial: such as cloud computing, pharmacies, and computing products (like social media platforms or GPT wrappers). These bring existing capabilities to specific markets, or at scale.

My robotics work tends to fall into the applied category, where the difficulty in buying parts can be likened to the difficulty of choosing existing theory to utilize and improve upon. That is—in a more general sense, buying robotics parts is hard because we are dictating a general strategy to get to new capabilities implicitly in our purchases. Note that this extends to other areas, too: the hardest part of theory is looking for insights into making new methods work, and industrially, business and growth strategy dictate a product’s life and death. So don’t be afraid to plan—once you’re done, you’re already halfway there.

Endnote: Got a cool robotics project idea, or want to get involved in robotics at Stanford? Shoot us an email at stanfordroboclub@gmail.com or visit our website!

item.title: Foreign Language Games of Mafia
item.description: A survivor's guide (and the importance of writing)
item.dc:creator: Andy Tang
item.content:encoded:
IF 12 is the wolf, then high probability that 8 is wolf??
6/9/5/3
12 wolf, then (1,2,8,11,13 possibly wolf?)

— Notes from recent Mafia game

Most people are familiar with Mafia/Werewolf, but I’m pretty sure only China has a massive game show focused solely on professional Mafia players. The game (狼人杀, a variant of Werewolf) has an infinitude of variations from chaotic to logical, with the core concept that the townspeople need to kill all the werewolves to win whereas the werewolves win by either killing all the gods (townspeople with powers) or villagers (those without).

As a non-Chinese person with basic fluency in Chinese, I was invited last year to a game at an international friend’s birthday party. The setting was uniquely intoxicating: part debate, part logic puzzle, part psychological drama, elevated by the fact that it was being played by some of the brightest math and computer science students at Stanford. I was hooked.

Now, after almost a year playing these games, one thing uniquely stands out to me: my skill drastically improves when I take notes. I’ve won three out of both the five games I’ve journaled and the more than a dozen that I didn’t. Moreover, I qualitatively feel far more on top of the game when I keep notes. Why?

The Slow Loop

My belief is that note-taking under stress activates a slower, reflective loop in my mind which helps integrate the tactical messaging I’m getting from players around the table. While it’s easy for me to buy even an incoherent narrative in isolation, keeping track of the relative plausibility of thirteen or more lines of reasoning can really only be done on paper. The foreign language aspect of these Mafia games make this uniquely apparent: while my brain can multitask in English, merely understanding and formulating speeches in Chinese takes up the vast majority of my thinking in these rapid-fire foreign-language exchanges.

I think I enjoy the same benefit in other games of strategy. For example, keeping a game journal in the incredibly manipulative and zero-sum game of Diplomacy often helps me gain a better understanding of intentions and positions across the game board. I suspect that these ideas probably apply to all social/strategy-focused games with several players. Indeed, if we broaden our definitions, it probably applies to many areas of life, e.g.:

  • Situations in which one or more parties may not have incentives aligned with good-faith negotiation, where journaling can uncover underlying values or strategic considerations which might motivate counterparty actions.

  • Complex systems where multiple “players” might act in an emergent and unpredictable manner. Examples might include biological ecosystems, foreign policy, businesses, or community organizations. Journaling might guide an actor to filter for high-quality information and find the correct questions to ask of their current situation (which derive the actions they should take).

  • Reflection upon the past: there are myriad causes for outrage at all times in the age of the Internet, often stuck in a present where one can find themselves deeply emotionally caught up in a situation. Journaling can help one find distance from the situation and evaluate conflicting information sources, allowing a more rational judgement beyond present-day moral fluctuations.

Endnote: One of my dubious “honors” involves being in the Discord server where Meta AI conducted a clandestine benchmark of their CICERO Diplomacy agent, which achieved expert human performance at the game. I wonder how this same reflective-information gathering might manifest in large foundation models for strategic thinking, and if not whether it could be used to boost existing reasoning performance.

item.title: Systems III: Commoditization
item.description: Reflections on a summer of corn and code
item.dc:creator: Andy Tang
item.content:encoded:
Whatever its social form may be, wealth always consists of use-values, which in the first instance are not affected by this form. From the taste of wheat it is not possible to tell who produced it, a Russian serf, a French peasant or an English capitalist.

— Karl Marx, Zur Kritik der Politischen Ökonomie

Have you ever imagined corn growing? Maybe it is a Midwestern thing to do. The first sprouts in spring are small. Over the years the stalks grow taller and firmer, eventually bearing a golden crown and ears of corn seed. In these ears silks form first, maturing into white blisters of fluid, maturing into yellow starchy kernels. After the corn dries some more the combine comes through one day and the field is barren once more.

As a kid in Central Illinois, it’s impossible to escape corn and soybeans: I live next to several fields. These commodities were made even more escapable by my beloved mother, who would quiz me with Fermi questions like a drill sergeant. Every year the Chicago Mercantile Exchange numbers come in like Christmas presents. “How many lean hog were slaughtered in America this week? What’s the price of a barrel of Brent crude?” All par for the course in my household.

Commoditizing the World

It is obvious that corn is a commodity. No one but the scientists and farmers care about the growth patterns and harvesting of corn: we just care about the eating, and one corn kernel is as good as the other. How many other things are commodities? For example: at my software engineering job, my boss cares more about whether the feature is written than whether I write the feature. Is this labor a commodity?

Perhaps not; in the long tail of unforeseeable events there are always crises requiring a specific caliber of engineer or a specific brand of management. There is enough noise and few enough people here that these things can be described as unique. But it seems like much of the day-to-day job of software engineering is commoditizable.

At larger scale it strikes me that many of our technological revolutions seem to commoditize. The Agricultural Revolution commoditized food, while the Industrial Revolution did so for manufactured goods. The Financial Revolution of capitalism (e.g. mass lending, actuarial tables, joint-stock companies) commoditized risk and reward in business ventures. The Internet may have commoditized information (and certainly commoditized attention, as Tim Hwang notes in the wonderful Subprime Attention Crisis). It seems almost certain that AI will commoditize intelligence to some degree, as is already proven with tutors like Khanmigo.

We are commoditizing the world. In some ways this makes it more predictable, more reassuring: we are never guessing about the quality of our oranges. Yet perhaps there is something lost here too. There are a billion stories, a billion golden crowns of corn, forgotten under the tyranny of a single standardized result. In controlling the world, are we imprisoning ourselves?

Endnote: I also wonder about what might never be commoditized. One such thing might be great art. In her 2014 essay, Taylor Swift certainly makes such an argument in the face of declining profits from music streaming—and if anything present events are a vindication. Human connection is another thing that is difficult to bottle up or even value: such a thing disappears at a concerted effort to extract it.

item.title: Systems II: Focus from Limits
item.dc:creator: Andy Tang
item.content:encoded:
Fear is the mind-killer. Fear is the little-death that brings total obliteration. I will face my fear. I will permit it to pass over me and through me. And when it has gone past I will turn the inner eye to see its path. Where the fear has gone there will be nothing. Only I will remain.

— Frank Herbert, Dune (emphasis my own)

“I am large, I contain multitudes,” Whitman writes, yet I feel the weight of the world as it makes me small. I know it is impossible to “be large” if the weight of the world constricts me: the weight of my fear and greed.

How can I know myself when I am small, boxed, and afraid? I cannot. So I use pain and immersion to break me free of these chains. Sometimes I am running from these concerns, sometimes I am escaping them in reading, often I seek my demons directly. I write here about that seeking.

Against Fear

Here I take from the Stoics and their memento mori. “Light is the left hand of darkness and darkness the right hand of light.” Half the world is night; thus to shrink away from darkness dooms you to half-blindness. Imagine your obituary if you died tomorrow. What would be on it? Can you read it without any regret?

Perhaps these contemplations are my greatest bulwark against fear. By acknowledging the possibility of imminent death, my beliefs are shaped to bear such a risk. For example, this examination of death is the very reason I have come to value the efforts I make as ends in themselves, rather than means to an ever-distant aim.

Against Greed

I find that much of my greed is mundane: the kind of greed that leads us to seek a foundation in an uncertain world. One of my favorite tricks is to imagine satisfying this greed. The average cost of an international vacation is $271 per day. Hence, to take a four-person family on such a vacation for every day of the year would be $395,660. The average return on the S&P 500 is somewhere above 10%: assume your investments make 8% a year and there’s a 20% capital gains tax. This means you’d need just south of $6 million to go on an endless vacation based on passive income alone.

I ask people (and myself) what they would do with $6 million, and summarize their responses below:

  1. The Homemaker: This is most common, and involves something like settling down, having a family, etc. This is also the most likely category to mention that it’s very important to get financial advice on their windfall.

  2. The Traveller: The second most common (I believe categories 1 and 2 together cover 80% of those I have asked this question to). These people would take the endless vacation described previously. A lot of creatives seem to prefer this route to sample the full range of experiences the world has to offer.

  3. The Architect: My category and in my opinion the most taxing. These people seek to use their money as a foundation to take greater risks and make a greater impact than they would otherwise. For a lot of Stanford kids, that means startups, but I’ve talked to others in this category who want to dedicate themselves to great art and writing.

  4. The Patron: Only two friends have ever replied to me in this vein. Similar to VCs, people of this typology believe that others can use their money to more effectively change the world. I think people of this type are so rare because it takes profound humility to both willingly spend your money on others and accept that you aren’t the one who will use it best.

Endnote: I think the motivations people take to get to these conclusions may serve as a secondary typology of these categories themselves. I am motivated by a sense of responsibility to change an imperfect world for the better. Others may be motivated by their comfort and fulfillment, a commitment to community, an aesthetic desire for beauty, human self-esteem from achievement, or many other reasons.

I hope to carry out a larger, single-question online survey to see if people outside my sample group have similar patterns. I also am interested in how these patterns change based on gender, ethnicity, and age.

item.title: Systems I: Practical Ethics
item.description: Eudaimonia and the process of finding things out
item.dc:creator: Andy Tang
item.content:encoded:
Unverfügbarkeit: what does it mean? [...] It is not about non-predictability, but non-engineerability. There is no way to “fabricate” resonance, to instrumentally bring it about.

[...]

The first guiding thesis in this work I would like to develop in this essay is that, for late modern human beings, the world has become a point of aggression. 

— Hartmut Rosa, The Uncontrollability of the World

I find it striking how many classical philosophers describe morality clinically, without regard to the emotion and intensity of the human experience. One camp of philosophers, the utilitarians, argue morals are means to some single end (happiness, fulfillment1, etc.) Deontology, in contrast, bases its ethics around unyielding universal rules. Within this context, I meditate on my imperfect ethics, spurred by an abnormally relaxed day and long run.

Meditation

Today I let myself sit idly alone for the first time in weeks. For the past month, my mind has been water sloshed this way and that in the Silicon Valley reality distortion field. Today my water is a mirror again. I am unsettled at what I have become.

Every unthinking interaction may bring great import. Yet every splash I make feels so insignificant. The world is small. The world is big. Life is short. Life is long. It is so easy to get lost.

Through idleness, I made space for many things I didn’t do this month. I spent the entire afternoon calling my parents. I blasted Linkin Park and Les Mis. I coded something just for fun and went on a seven-mile run. It feels like I am returning to a duty I have neglected but always had.

Expostulation

What is virtue? Nietzsche calls it a chain. Bentham argues it is the maximization of happiness. Kant insists it must be a universal law. Philosophers war over right and wrong. Few speak to what is human2.

Sift a sunset through the finest sieve and tell me, sages, where is an iota of utility? An atom of imperative? Speak to me: what judgment may I cast when so many things are unspeakable, unknowable?

I am no machine or Ubermensch. Sages: your descriptions are lofty peaks of perfection that I cannot climb. Forgive me, Nietzsche, I will need a chain to guide me. Forgive me, Bentham, I will only hurt myself if I see others as means to an end. Forgive me, Kant. My rules are ever-changing and flawed. They teach me what matters. They help me make better rules. Through this process, I’ve tried to find human alignment: a set of values that best fit me.

Endnote: I do find it interesting, as an uninformed spectator, that effective altruism seems to focus purely on utilitarianism and mechanisms of control over AI.

Thanks for reading Steel and Silicon! Subscribe for free to receive new posts.

1

Fulfillment is not happiness and I will die on this hill. What it is is much harder to describe. For myself, I’ve found that it comes from learning new things and working on hard problems. That’s why I try to stay on that path.

2

This is why I like Bernard Williams so much, and I’m sure some of the ideas in this essay are inspired by him. He didn’t try to build his own system of ethics, but that’s what made him so special. He didn’t stick to a precise logical definition of ethics, but rather attacked that same clean-room purity, arguing that real life is far too complex to be captured by a single canned system.
